title: Λέων καὶ ταῦρος
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 211. Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« »). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Λέων ταύρῳ παμμεγέθει ἐπιβουλεύων ἐβουλήθη δόλῳ αὐτοῦ περιγενέσθαι.
sentences.tr: Leōn taurōi pammegethei epibouleuōn eboulēthē dolōi autou perigenesthai.
sentences.l: A lion, plotting against an enormous bull, resolved by a trick to get-the-better-of him.
sentences.n: ἐπιβουλεύω takes the dative of the one plotted against; περιγίγνομαι takes the genitive of the one got the better of. The lion's whole strategy is announced in the first line: δόλῳ, by a trick, because open force will not serve against a bull of that size.

sentences.t: Διόπερ πρόβατον τεθυκέναι φήσας ἐφ’ ἑστίασιν αὐτὸν ἐκάλεσε, βουλόμενος κατακλιθέντα αὐτὸν καταγωνίσασθαι.
sentences.tr: Dioper probaton tethykenai phēsas eph’ hestiasin auton ekalese, boulomenos kataklithenta auton katagōnisasthai.
sentences.l: Wherefore, having-said that he had-sacrificed a sheep, he called him to a feast, wishing, once he had-lain-down, to overpower him.
sentences.i: So, claiming to have sacrificed a sheep, he invited him to a feast, meaning to master him once he had taken his place at table.
sentences.n: θύω is to sacrifice, and sacrifice is what put meat on a Greek table — announcing a victim is the ordinary way of announcing a dinner. κατακλίνομαι is to recline at the meal: the aorist participle κατακλιθέντα marks precisely the moment the guest is off his feet and helpless.

sentences.t: Ὁ δὲ ἐλθὼν καὶ θεασάμενος λέβητάς τε πολλοὺς καὶ ὀβελίσκους μεγάλους, τὸ δὲ πρόβατον οὐδαμοῦ, μηδὲν εἰπὼν ἀπηλλάττετο.
sentences.tr: Ho de elthōn kai theasamenos lebētas te pollous kai obeliskous megalous, to de probaton oudamou, mēden eipōn apēllatteto.
sentences.l: And he, having-come and having-seen both many cauldrons and great spits, but the sheep nowhere, saying nothing was-departing.
sentences.i: The bull came, and saw many cauldrons and great spits — and no sheep anywhere — and went off without a word.
sentences.n: The chain of aorist participles carrying the action forward is the engine of these fables; you will meet it constantly. The evidence is a matter of scale: a sheep needs one pot, and what stands ready here is equipment for something far larger.

sentences.t: Τοῦ δὲ λέοντος αἰτιωμένου αὐτὸν καὶ τὴν αἰτίαν πυνθανομένου δι’ ἣν οὐδὲν δεινὸν παθὼν ἄλογος ἄπεισιν, ἔφη· « Ἀλλ’ ἔγωγε οὐ μάτην τοῦτο ποιῶ· ὁρῶ γὰρ παρασκευὴν οὐχὶ ὡς εἰς πρόβατον, ἀλλ’ εἰς ταῦρον ἡτοιμασμένην. »
sentences.tr: Tou de leontos aitiōmenou auton kai tēn aitian pynthanomenou di’ hēn ouden deinon pathōn alogos apeisin, ephē· « All’ egōge ou matēn touto poiō· horō gar paraskeuēn ouchi hōs eis probaton, all’ eis tauron hētoimasmenēn. »
sentences.l: And the lion blaming him and inquiring the reason on account of which, having-suffered nothing dreadful, he goes off without-a-word, he said: « But I for my part do not do this in vain; for I see a preparation made-ready not as for a sheep, but for a bull. »
sentences.i: When the lion reproached him and asked the reason why he was going off without a word, having suffered no harm, the bull said: « I do not do it for nothing: the preparations I see are made ready not for a sheep but for a bull. »
sentences.n: A genitive absolute (τοῦ λέοντος αἰτιωμένου … πυνθανομένου) sets the whole frame of the question. ἄλογος is literally "wordless", picking up the μηδὲν εἰπών of the sentence before; the same adjective also means "unreasoning", and the Greek lets both senses stand at once. οὐ μάτην is "not for nothing, not without cause". ἡτοιμασμένην is a perfect passive participle agreeing with παρασκευήν — the preparation stands there already made.

sentences.t: Ὁ λόγος δηλοῖ ὅτι τοὺς φρονίμους τῶν ἀνθρώπων αἱ τῶν πονηρῶν τέχναι οὐ λανθάνουσιν.
sentences.tr: Ho logos dēloi hoti tous phronimous tōn anthrōpōn hai tōn ponērōn technai ou lanthanousin.
sentences.l: The story shows that the contrivances of the wicked do not escape the notice of the prudent among men.
sentences.n: λανθάνω takes the accusative of the person whose notice is escaped, so τοὺς φρονίμους is the object and αἱ τέχναι the subject — the reverse of the English arrangement. τῶν ἀνθρώπων is partitive: the prudent among men. τέχνη here is not skill in the honourable sense but the contrivance, the dodge.
